topics.title: Why does a car engine need an electric motor just to start?

cards.title: Once it's running, it keeps itself going for hours.
cards.text: Press start, and a small electric motor turns the engine for a moment before it runs by itself.
cards.hook: So how does burning petrol turn an engine at all?

cards.title: Hot gas pushes a sliding plug that turns a shaft
cards.text: Inside, petrol and air burn in a metal tube called a cylinder. The hot gas pushes a sliding plug, the piston, along the tube. A rod links the piston to a bent shaft. Each push turns the shaft, like your leg on a bike pedal.
cards.hook: But can the piston push every time it moves?

cards.title: The piston makes four moves, and only one pushes
cards.text: First it pulls fuel and air in, then squeezes them tight. Then a spark lights them. Packed tight, the burning gas pushes the piston much harder. Last, it clears the used gas out of the engine.
cards.hook: So what moves the piston for the other three?

cards.title: The turning shaft drags the piston through the other three
cards.text: At the start nothing is turning yet, so nothing can drag it. The electric motor turns the shaft until a spark lights the first squeezed load.
cards.hook: So once it's going, what keeps the shaft turning?

steps.note: The motor pulls fuel and air in
The push: the motor lets go

cards.title: A heavy wheel keeps the shaft turning between pushes
cards.text: Its weight carries the piston through the other three moves. And several cylinders take turns, so the pushes come close together and the engine runs smoothly.
cards.takeaway: An engine can only push once it has pulled in and squeezed its fuel, so something else turns it first.

cards.note: The first engine to squeeze its fuel and air before lighting it was built by Nicolaus Otto in Germany in 1876, and it ran far better than every engine before it. Engines that squeeze their fuel and air and work in four moves still run on what's called the Otto cycle.

topics.title: Why does one gear click make the same hill feel easier?

cards.title: Same hill, same legs.
cards.text: On a steep hill you push as hard as you can and barely move. Click the gear lever once and the same hill feels easier. Your legs aren't stronger, and the hill isn't flatter.
cards.hook: So what does the lever change at the back wheel?

steps.note: You push as hard as you can and barely move
Click the gear lever: the same hill feels easier

cards.title: A smaller back ring spins the wheel more for each pedal turn
cards.text: The chain runs from the pedal ring to a stack of rings on the back wheel. The lever slides it onto another ring. Each link fits one tooth, so a ring with fewer teeth turns more times for the same length of chain.
cards.hook: So how far does one pedal turn carry you?

steps.note: The chain runs from the pedal ring to a back ring
The lever slides the chain onto another ring

cards.title: A smaller back ring carries you farther with each pedal turn
cards.text: More wheel turns means each pedal turn carries you farther. With a bigger back ring, each turn takes you a shorter way.
cards.hook: So why does a shorter way per turn make the hill feel easier?

steps.note: One pedal turn, smaller back ring: farther
One pedal turn, bigger back ring: a shorter way

cards.title: A shorter way per turn means a lighter push, and more turns to the top
cards.text: Think of walking up a steep path. Long strides are hard heaves, short quick steps are light, and you reach the same top either way. A pedal turn is like a stride, and the hill is the same height in every gear. So each turn lifts you only a little way up, and the push can be light.
cards.hook: But what about on flat road?

cards.title: To go the same speed on flat road, a smaller back ring means slower pedalling
cards.text: To go the same speed, a smaller back ring means pedalling slower, with a harder push each time. On flat road that's fine, because legs push best in a narrow range of pedalling speeds.
cards.takeaway: A gear can't make the hill any lower. It only decides how many pushes it takes to climb it.

steps.note: Bigger back ring: your legs spin fast, each push is light
Smaller back ring: slower pedalling, a harder push

cards.note: Before chains, the pedals of the old penny-farthing were fixed straight to the hub of the huge front wheel, so there were no gears at all: one pedal turn was one wheel turn, and the only way to go farther per turn was a bigger wheel, up to about 60 inches across. The chain and a smaller back ring let a smaller wheel go as far as a big one, and that is the idea your gear lever still plays with. Even today the word "gear inches" means how wide a penny-farthing wheel would have to be to match your gear.

topics.title: Can your skin feel wet when it is dry?

cards.title: Your skin has no sensor made just for wet.
cards.text: Your skin has tiny nerve endings, called sensors, that react to things such as cold, warmth and touch. But scientists have looked for one and found none made just for wet.
cards.hook: So what do your sensors feel when water touches you?

steps.note: Tiny sensors react to cold, warmth and touch
No sensor made just for wet

cards.title: Water cooler than your skin takes heat out of it, and your cold sensors notice
cards.text: When something wet touches you, water cooler than your skin takes heat out of it fast. Your cold sensors notice your skin getting colder and send a cold signal to your brain.
cards.hook: But is a cold signal all it takes to feel wet?

steps.note: Water cooler than your skin takes heat out of it
Your cold sensors notice and send a cold signal to your brain

cards.title: Your brain puts a cold signal and a close, even touch together into wet
cards.text: A wet thing also gives your skin a close, even touch, and your touch sensors feel it. Your brain puts the cold signal and the touch together into wet.
cards.hook: So could a dry finger feel wet?

steps.note: A wet thing also gives your skin a close, even touch
Your brain puts the cold signal and the touch together into wet

cards.title: In 1900, a dry finger in a thin rubber sheath felt wet in water
cards.text: So you can feel wet when you are dry. In 1900, a psychologist covered a finger with a thin rubber sheath, like a glove for one finger. The finger was then lowered into water, and it stayed dry but felt wet. The people who tried it at first refused to believe the finger was dry. In the same test, warmer water felt less wet, and lukewarm water barely at all.
cards.takeaway: Wet is not a sense of its own. Your brain builds it from cold and touch.

steps.note: A finger in a thin rubber sheath
The finger stays dry, but it feels wet

cards.note: Some animals do have a sensor for how damp the air is, which people do not. Fruit flies keep humidity sensors in their antennae, and mosquitoes have two kinds on theirs: one that reacts to dry air and one to damp air. Up close the sensors help a mosquito tell a person is near, and the damp-air kind helps it find water to lay eggs in. They sense water vapour in the air, not the feeling of a wet surface.

topics.title: Why is the sky blue at noon and red at sunset?

cards.title: It's the same sky and the same Sun.
cards.text: Sunlight looks yellow, but it's really all colours mixed together. Air looks clear, but it isn't quite. So how does clear air turn sunlight into a blue sky, and later an orange one?

cards.title: Sunlight is every colour at once
cards.text: After rain, a rainbow shows what is hiding in sunlight: every colour, mixed together. Light travels in tiny waves, and each colour has its own length. Red waves are long and stretched out. Blue waves are short and close together. So what does the air do to these waves?

cards.title: Clear air still bounces blue light
cards.text: Air looks like nothing, but it's made of gases. The gases are tiny particles, too small to see. Sunlight hits them all the time, and each hit sends the light off in a new direction. Short blue waves bounce much more often than long red ones: about 5 times as much. So where does all that bounced blue go?

cards.title: Bounced blue comes at you from everywhere
cards.text: Particles fill the whole sky, not only the part near the Sun. Each one bounces some blue toward your eyes, so you see blue wherever you look. The sky has no blue of its own. It's sunlight, bounced toward you by the air. So why does that blue sky turn orange at sunset?

cards.title: At sunset, light crosses far more air
cards.text: Air is a thin layer around Earth. When the Sun is overhead, its light takes a short path down through the layer. At sunset, the Sun is near the horizon, so its light must cross the layer sideways. That is a much longer trip, through about 40 times more air. On the way, the particles bounce away most of the blue, so mostly red and orange reaches your eyes.
cards.takeaway: Short trip: blue sky; long trip: red sunset.

steps.note: Noon: a short trip through air
Blue bounced away, red gets through

cards.note: The Sun looks yellow because the air has already bounced some blue out of its light. Violet bounces even more than blue, but the Sun gives out less violet and our eyes see it poorly, so the sky looks blue, not violet.

topics.title: How does your phone find you with no mobile signal?

cards.title: Zero bars, and your phone still finds you.
cards.text: Out in the open, with no mobile signal at all, your phone still finds you. It doesn't need to call anyone. It only listens.
cards.hook: So what radio signal is it listening to?

steps.note: Your phone has no mobile signal
It never calls anyone. It only listens

cards.title: Satellites keep sending a radio signal that says where they are and when it was sent
cards.text: Satellites circle Earth far above you, and each one keeps sending out a radio signal. The signal says where the satellite is and what time it was sent. Your phone catches it and sends nothing back.
cards.hook: So how does the time a radio signal was sent tell your phone a distance?

steps.note: A satellite keeps sending out a radio signal
It says where it is and what time it was sent
Your phone catches it and sends nothing back

cards.title: The gap between when a radio signal was sent and when it arrived is a distance
cards.text: Count the seconds from lightning to thunder, and the wait tells you how far away the storm is. A satellite's radio signal is far faster than sound, but its delay is a distance too. From straight overhead it arrives in about 0.07 seconds, shorter than a blink. Your phone compares when it was sent with when it arrived. That gap, times the speed of light, is the distance.
cards.hook: So how many satellites does it take to pin down your spot?

steps.note: The wait from lightning to thunder tells you how far away the storm is
The gap, times the speed of light, is the distance

cards.title: With three satellites, only two spots fit, and only one is on Earth
cards.text: One distance leaves a whole ring of places you could be, all the same distance from that satellite. With three satellites, only two spots fit all three distances, and only one of them is on Earth. The other is far out in space.
cards.hook: But how exact is your phone's own clock?

steps.note: One distance leaves a whole ring of places you could be
With three satellites, only two spots fit
Only one of them is on Earth

cards.title: Your phone's own clock isn't exact, so it listens to a fourth satellite
cards.text: One problem is left. Your phone times the arrival with its own clock, and that clock is nowhere near as exact as a satellite's. A clock a millionth of a second wrong puts you about 300 metres off. So the phone listens to a fourth satellite. That lets it work out how wrong its own clock is, and fix it.
cards.takeaway: Your phone doesn't need to call anyone. It listens to satellites and turns the delay into where you are.

steps.note: Your phone's clock isn't as exact, so you land about 300 metres off
A fourth satellite shows it how wrong its clock is
It fixes its own clock and lands on the right spot

cards.note: The satellites' clocks are set to tick a little slower before launch. Up there, far from Earth's pull and moving fast, they would otherwise run about 38 millionths of a second ahead of clocks on the ground every day, and that would pile up into a position error of about 11 kilometres a day. Engineers fixed this before launch by changing how fast the clocks tick, one of the few places where Einstein's ideas about time are used by something in your pocket.

topics.title: Why isn't the shop paid the moment you tap your card?

cards.title: You tap, it beeps, and you walk away.
cards.text: Tapping your card feels like paying. But the card reader only sends a short message asking your bank if this card can pay.
cards.hook: So where does that message go before it comes back with a yes?

steps.note: The reader sends a short message: can this card pay?

cards.title: The message goes to the shop's bank, then a card network, then your bank
cards.text: The reader's message reaches the shop's bank. That bank passes it to a card network, a company such as Visa or Mastercard that links banks. The network passes it to your bank, which answers yes or no. The answer travels back the same way, in a couple of seconds.
cards.hook: So when your bank says yes, does the shop get the money?

steps.note: The message goes to the shop's bank, then a card network, then your bank
The yes comes back the same way

cards.title: Your bank's yes is a promise to pay, and the money hasn't reached the shop yet
cards.text: Your bank checks that the card is real and that you have enough money or credit. If so, it takes that amount off what you can spend straight away. So you can't spend the same money twice. But the money hasn't reached the shop yet.
cards.hook: So why does the shop have to wait to be paid?

steps.note: This is what you can spend
The yes takes the amount off what you can spend
The money hasn't reached the shop yet

cards.title: Banks move money in totals, so the shop is usually paid a few working days later
cards.text: Banks don't move money for every single tap. They gather many payments and add them up, and the shop's bank is paid in totals. So the shop is usually paid a few working days after your tap.
cards.takeaway: The yes comes back in seconds, and the shop is usually paid a few working days later.

steps.note: Banks add many payments up into totals
A few working days later the totals reach the shop

cards.note: The shop gets a little less than you paid, because a small fee is shared among your bank, the card network and the shop's bank. The fee that goes to your bank is called the interchange fee.

topics.title: How can your phone name a song from a few noisy seconds?

cards.title: It picks one song out of millions, with people talking over it.
cards.text: All it gets is a few seconds of chatter with music somewhere inside.
cards.hook: So what does it keep, and what does it throw away?

cards.title: It draws the sound and keeps only the loudest dots
cards.text: On the chart, time runs left to right and high notes sit higher. The louder a sound, the brighter its dot. It keeps only the dots brighter than everything right around them, and throws the rest away. They're the hardest for chatter to cover up.
cards.hook: But one dot is just one note, and nearly every song has that. So what's rarer?

cards.title: A pair of notes is much rarer than one
cards.text: So it joins each dot to a few dots just after it. Each pair is two notes and the exact gap between them. It writes each pair down as a short code.
cards.hook: So how does it find the songs with your codes?

steps.note: One note: in nearly every song
Joined to dots just after it

cards.title: A giant list shows every song with each code
cards.text: The app's makers turned every song they have into codes ahead of time. The list works like a book's index, giving each song with that code and the moment it turns up.
cards.hook: But one code points at lots of songs. So which is the right one?

cards.title: In the right song, many of your codes line up
cards.text: In wrong songs, a few codes match but turn up scattered. In the right one, they come in the same order, as far apart in time as in those few seconds.
cards.takeaway: It never listens for the words or the tune, only for where the loudest dots sit.

cards.note: In 2002 it wasn't an app. You dialled 2580, held your phone up to the music, and a text message came back with the song and the singer.

topics.title: Why does one Moon give most beaches two high tides a day?

cards.title: There's only one Moon, and it's on one side of the sky at a time.
cards.text: The Moon pulls the sea toward it, so you'd expect one high tide a day. But most beaches get two.
cards.hook: So how does the Moon's pull make a second high tide?

cards.title: The Moon pulls the near sea harder than the ground, and the far sea less
cards.text: The Moon pulls harder on whatever is closer. So the sea facing it, the near sea, is pulled harder than the ground. The sea on the far side, the far sea, is pulled less hard than the ground.
cards.hook: So where does all that pulling make the sea pile up?

steps.note: The near sea is pulled most
The far sea is pulled least

cards.title: The sea piles up on both sides of Earth, in two bulges
cards.text: Picture three runners in a line. One magnet ahead pulls them all, the front one hardest and the back one least. The front runner is the near sea, the middle one the ground, the back one the far sea. The near sea is pulled ahead of the ground, and the ground is pulled ahead of the far sea. So the sea piles up on both sides of Earth, in two bulges.
cards.hook: So what happens to your beach as Earth turns?

steps.note: The front one is pulled hardest
The sea piles up on both sides

cards.title: As Earth turns under the bulges, your beach gets two high tides
cards.text: The bulges stay lined up with the Moon while Earth turns once a day beneath them. Your beach passes under one, then the other. That's two high tides, a bit over twelve hours apart.
cards.hook: But why does each day's high tide come a little later?

cards.title: The Moon moves on, so each day's high tide comes about 50 minutes later
cards.text: The Moon also moves round Earth the way Earth spins. So each day your beach needs about 50 extra minutes to catch up with it.
cards.takeaway: One Moon stretches the sea on both sides of Earth, and Earth turns your beach through both.

steps.note: A day later the Moon has moved on
The beach needs about 50 extra minutes

cards.note: A tide is really a very slow wave moving through the sea, and in each ocean it circles a point where the sea hardly rises or falls at all, called an amphidromic point. That is why high tide never lines up neatly with the Moon overhead. In 1687 Isaac Newton explained tides as the pull of the Moon and Sun on the sea.

topics.title: In a room of 23, what's the chance two share a birthday?

cards.title: Take a guess before you read on.
cards.text: Many people guess a small chance, but it's about 50%. A true fact that sounds wrong is called a paradox, and this one is the birthday paradox.
cards.hook: So why does 50% feel so wrong?

cards.title: It feels wrong because we think of our own birthday
cards.text: Walk into a room of 22 strangers, and the chance someone shares your birthday is less than 6%.
cards.hook: But does the match have to include you?

cards.title: The match doesn't have to include you
cards.text: If all 23 of you shook hands once with each other, there'd be 253 handshakes. Each handshake is a pair who could share a birthday, and only 22 of them include you.
cards.hook: So what do all those pairs do to the chance?

cards.title: More pairs means a higher chance of a match
cards.text: Any one pair almost never matches. But 253 pairs push the chance of a match to about 50%.
cards.hook: So what happens as more people walk in?

cards.title: Pairs pile up fast
cards.text: Each new person makes a new pair with everyone already in the room. By 57 people there are 1,596 pairs, and the chance of a match is over 99%.
cards.takeaway: Count the pairs, not the people.

cards.note: At the 2014 football World Cup, each squad had 23 players, and about half the squads had two players with the same birthday. To get a 50% chance that a stranger shares your birthday, you'd need 253 strangers, the same number as the pairs in a room of 23. Real rooms match a little more often, because births aren't spread evenly across the year.

topics.title: Why is it summer when Earth is farthest from the Sun?

cards.title: Summer feels like the Sun has come closer.
cards.text: But in early July, while Europe and the USA have summer, Earth is at its farthest from the Sun. In early January, in their winter, it's at its closest.
cards.hook: So is it much farther away in July than in January?

cards.title: Earth is only about 3 percent farther in July than in January
cards.text: And when Australia has summer, Canada has winter, at the same distance from the Sun. So distance can't be it.
cards.hook: So if it isn't distance, what is it?

cards.title: Each half of Earth takes a turn leaning toward the Sun
cards.text: Earth leans about 23 degrees from upright, like a classroom globe, and the lean always points toward the same faraway spot. So in June the north half leans toward the Sun, and in December, on the other side of its trip, it leans away. The south half does the opposite.
cards.hook: But why would leaning toward the Sun make it warmer?

steps.note: June: north leans in, December: north leans away

cards.title: Leaning toward the Sun packs its light into a smaller patch
cards.text: Shine a torch straight down at a table and you get a small, bright spot. Tilt it, and the same light spreads into a long, dim patch. The half leaning toward the Sun gets light more like the straight beam, so each bit of ground warms more.
cards.hook: Does the lean change anything else?

steps.note: Straight: small bright spot, tilted: long dim patch

cards.title: The lean also makes summer days longer
cards.text: It puts more of that half on the sunny side as Earth spins. In London, a June day is about twice as long as a December one.
cards.takeaway: Summer doesn't come when Earth is closer to the Sun. It comes when your half leans toward it.

steps.note: London: long day in June, short day in December

cards.note: At the North Pole, the Sun stays up for about six months, then come months of twilight and dark. The same lean does it.

topics.title: Why doesn't instant glue stick inside its own tube?

cards.title: It goes hard on your fingers in seconds.
cards.text: But it can sit in its tube for months and stay runny.
cards.hook: So what is it waiting for?

cards.title: Superglue goes hard when it touches water
cards.text: White school glue goes hard as its water dries away. Superglue works the other way round. Even the moisture in the air is enough to make it go hard.
cards.hook: So where does it find water on your fingers?

cards.title: Your skin carries a thin film of water
cards.text: It's too thin to feel, and almost everything around you has one too. When superglue lands on it, the glue touches water straight away. That's why it goes hard on your fingers in seconds.
cards.hook: So why doesn't it go hard inside the tube?

cards.title: A sealed tube lets no water in
cards.text: So the glue inside just waits, runny, for months. Leave the cap off, though, and moisture from the air creeps in. The glue at the tip goes hard and blocks it.
cards.takeaway: School glue goes hard when water leaves. Superglue goes hard when water arrives.

cards.note: What does the water actually do? It makes the glue's tiny building blocks hook onto each other in long chains, and long chains can't flow. Makers also add a tiny dash of acid that stops any chain that starts by accident.
